short_definition: An exchange-traded fund (ETF) is a pooled investment fund that holds a basket of assets, such as stocks or bonds, and trades on a stock exchange like a single share.
explanation: An ETF collects money from many investors and uses it to buy a set of assets, often to track an index, sector, commodity or strategy. You buy and sell ETF shares through a brokerage account during market hours, and the price moves throughout the day as the underlying assets change in value.

ETFs matter to beginners because one purchase can give exposure to dozens or thousands of holdings, which makes diversification easier than buying each asset one by one. Many broad-market ETFs have relatively low ongoing costs, but fees vary widely, so always check the expense ratio and any trading commissions on the provider's and broker's sites.

The main trade-off is that an ETF is only as diversified and as safe as what it holds: a broad bond ETF and a leveraged single-sector ETF carry very different risks. ETFs can lose value, some trade with wide bid-ask spreads, and tax treatment differs by country, so check your local rules or a licensed adviser before deciding.
example: Illustrative example: Priya invests 500 in a hypothetical ETF that tracks 400 large companies. Instead of buying 400 separate stocks, she owns a small slice of all of them. If the index falls 10%, her holding would fall to roughly 450 before fees; if it rises 10%, roughly 550.
common_mistake: Assuming every ETF is a low-risk, diversified index fund — many ETFs are narrow, leveraged or inverse products designed for short-term trading and can lose value very quickly.
title: Exchange-Traded Fund (ETF)
